column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent;
whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest.” Reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned together belief in Allah and belief in the Last Day in these three matters

because belief in Allah is the foundation of everything that must be believed in, for anything that must be believed in follows from belief in Allah; and belief in the Last Day contains a reminder of the return and of recompense for deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

His words, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent”: this is one of his ﷺ comprehensive statements. It requires guarding the tongue from speaking except in what is good. Al-Nawawī said in his explanation of this hadith:
“Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him) said: The meaning of the hadith is that when he wants to speak, he should think: if it is clear that there is no harm in it for him, he speaks,
and if it is clear that there is harm in it, or he is in doubt about it, he refrains. The great imam Abū Muḥammad ibn Abī Zayd, the imam of the Mālikīs in the Maghrib in his time, said:
All the manners of goodness branch out from four hadiths: the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, ‘Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent’;
his ﷺ saying, ‘Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him’; his ﷺ saying to the one for whom he summarised his advice,

‘Do not become angry’; and his saying, ‘None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.’” Al-Nawawī also quoted someone as saying: “If you had to buy the paper for the recording angels, you would keep quiet about much of your speech.”
Khayr (good) is a noun whose opposite is evil (sharr); khayr also comes as a comparative (“better”) with its hamzah dropped. Both are combined in the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:
“O Prophet, say to the captives in your hands: If Allah knows any good (khayr) in your hearts, He will give you better (khayr) than what was taken from you” [al-Anfāl 8:70].

His words, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour”: the right of the neighbour is one of the emphasised rights owed by his neighbour. Many hadiths have come encouraging honouring the neighbour and warning against harming him or causing him injury,

among them the hadith of ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her): “Jibrīl kept enjoining me to treat the neighbour well until I thought he would make him an heir.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (6014) and Muslim (2624). And the hadith: “By Allah, he does not believe!
By Allah, he does not believe!”
They said: “Who, O Messenger of Allah?”
He said: “The one whose neighbour is not safe from his harm.” Reported by al-Bukhārī (6016) and Muslim (73).
Honouring him means that one's kindness reaches him and that he is safe from one's harm. Neighbours are of three kinds:
a Muslim neighbour who is a relative, who has three rights: the right of neighbourliness, the right of kinship and the right of Islam;
a Muslim neighbour who is not a relative, who has the right of Islam and of neighbourliness;
and a neighbour who is neither a Muslim nor a relative, who has the right of neighbourliness only.
The neighbour most deserving of kindness is the one whose door is closest,
because he sees what enters his neighbour's house and so looks forward to his kindness.

His words, “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest”: honouring the guest is one of the rights Muslims have over one another, and it is part of noble character. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (6019), from the hadith of Abū Shurayḥ, who said:

My ears heard and my eyes saw when the Prophet ﷺ spoke and said: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour; and whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his guest with his due (jāʾizah).” It was said: “And what is his due, O Messenger of Allah?”
He said: “A day and a night. Hospitality is three days, and whatever is beyond that is charity to him.”
Encouragement to speak about what is good.
Encouragement to remain silent if what one would say is not good.
Mentioning the Last Day when encouraging and warning,
since in it is the reckoning for deeds.
Encouragement to honour the neighbour, and a warning against harming him.
Urging to honour the guest and treat him well.
